questions.skill: Multiplying by powers of 10; equivalent calculations
questions.stem: Which of these does NOT give the same answer as 4.6 × 25?
questions.explanation: 4.6 × 25 = 115. If one number is made 10 times bigger and the other 10 times smaller, the answer stays the same, so the first three are equal. 25 = 100 ÷ 4, so 4.6 × 100 ÷ 4 also works. But 46 × 25 ÷ 100 = 1150 ÷ 100 = 11.5: 46 is 10 times bigger, but dividing by 100 makes it 100 times smaller.

distractors.D: didn't see that 25 = 100 ÷ 4

questions.skill: Rates and converting mL to L
questions.stem: A leaking tap drips 15 mL of water every minute. How much water is wasted in one full day?
questions.explanation: In one hour: 15 × 60 = 900 mL. In 24 hours: 900 × 24 = 21 600 mL. 1000 mL = 1 L, so that is 21.6 L.

questions.skill: Lowest common multiple over a time period
questions.stem: One lighthouse flashes every 12 seconds and another every 18 seconds. They flash together at exactly 9:00 pm. How many more times will they flash together before 9:05 pm?
questions.explanation: They flash together every 36 seconds (the lowest common multiple of 12 and 18). 5 minutes = 300 seconds. 300 ÷ 36 = 8 remainder 12, so they flash together 8 more times (at 36, 72, ... 288 seconds).

distractors.D: used 30 seconds

questions.skill: Division with a remainder: round up in context
questions.stem: 230 students are going on an excursion. Each bus holds 48 students and costs $350. What is the cheapest total cost for the buses?
questions.explanation: 230 ÷ 48 = 4 remainder 38. Four buses carry only 192 students, so 38 students need a fifth bus. 5 × $350 = $1750.

distractors.B: paid for 4.79 buses (part of a bus)
distractors.C: paid for part of a bus and rounded

questions.skill: Counting pairs without double-counting
questions.stem: Six friends meet. Each friend shakes hands with every other friend exactly once. How many handshakes are there?
questions.explanation: The first friend shakes 5 hands, the next shakes 4 new hands, then 3, 2, 1: 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15. (6 × 5 = 30 counts every handshake twice.)

questions.skill: From area to side length to perimeter
questions.stem: A square has an area of 64 cm². It is cut into 4 identical smaller squares. What is the total perimeter of the 4 smaller squares?
questions.explanation: 64 = 8 × 8, so the big square has sides of 8 cm. Each small square has sides of 4 cm and a perimeter of 16 cm. Four of them: 4 × 16 = 64 cm.

distractors.D: big perimeter + the two cut lines counted once

questions.skill: Difference of two fractions of the same whole
questions.stem: A jug is 3/4 full of water. After 600 mL is poured out, it is 1/3 full. How much water does the jug hold when it is full?
questions.explanation: The 600 mL is the difference between 3/4 and 1/3 of the jug. Use twelfths: 3/4 = 9/12 and 1/3 = 4/12, so 600 mL = 5/12. Then 1/12 = 120 mL, and the full jug is 12 × 120 = 1440 mL.

distractors.B: thought 600 mL is 3/4 of the jug
distractors.D: thought 600 mL is half the jug

questions.skill: Ordering from several clues
questions.stem:
Ari, Ben, Cy and Dan ran a race. There were no ties.
• Ari did not come first.
• Ben finished straight after Cy.
• Dan finished after Ben but before Ari.
Who came second?
questions.explanation: Ben comes straight after Cy, and Dan is after Ben but before Ari. So the order must be Cy, Ben, Dan, Ari. This fits 'Ari did not come first' too. Ben is second.

distractors.D: missed that Ben is straight after Cy

questions.skill: Using a mean (average) to find a missing score
questions.stem: Zara's first four test scores were 72, 80, 76 and 84. What must she score on her fifth test to have an average of exactly 80 across all five tests?
questions.explanation: For an average of 80 over 5 tests, the total must be 5 × 80 = 400. Her first four add to 312. She needs 400 − 312 = 88.

distractors.D: arithmetic slip adding the four scores

questions.skill: "For every 3 there are 5": a change makes them equal
questions.stem: In a box there are 3 red counters for every 5 blue counters. When 6 more red counters are added, there are the same number of red and blue counters. How many blue counters are there?
questions.explanation: Each 'group' has 3 red and 5 blue, so blue is ahead by 2 per group. 6 extra red closes the gap, so there are 6 ÷ 2 = 3 groups. Blue = 3 × 5 = 15 (red was 9, now 15).

distractors.A: gave the number of extra red counters
distractors.B: gave the number of red counters before
distractors.D: used 6 × 2

questions.skill: Counting weeks and days across months
questions.stem: A school term starts on Monday 25 January and lasts exactly 10 weeks. It is not a leap year. On what date is the last Friday of the term?
questions.explanation: The first Friday is 29 January. The last Friday is 9 weeks (63 days) later. After 29 January there are 2 days left in January and 28 in February, so 63 − 2 − 28 = 33 days into March: that is all 31 days of March plus 2 days, Friday 2 April.

distractors.D: added 10 full weeks to the start date (that is the Monday after the term)
distractors.E: counted 10 more weeks after the first Friday

questions.skill: Factors: which numbers have exactly 3 factors
questions.stem: The number 9 has exactly three factors: 1, 3 and 9. How many whole numbers from 1 to 50 have exactly three factors?
questions.explanation: Factors come in pairs, so a number has an odd number of factors only if it is a square number. Check the squares up to 50: 4 (1, 2, 4) ✓, 9 ✓, 16 (1, 2, 4, 8, 16) ✗, 25 ✓, 36 ✗, 49 (1, 7, 49) ✓. So 4, 9, 25 and 49: 4 numbers (squares of prime numbers).

distractors.D: counted all the square numbers up to 50

questions.skill: Two kinds of coins: count and total
questions.stem: Mia has only 20c and 50c coins. She has 14 coins worth $4.60 altogether. How many 50c coins does she have?
questions.explanation: If all 14 coins were 20c, she'd have $2.80. She has $1.80 more. Swapping a 20c coin for a 50c coin adds 30c, so she needs 180 ÷ 30 = 6 swaps: 6 fifty-cent coins (and 8 twenty-cent coins). Check: 6 × 50c + 8 × 20c = $3.00 + $1.60 = $4.60 ✓

distractors.D: guessed
